abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant Candidozyma auris (C. auris) has intensified the search for antifungal molecules with alternative structures and mechanisms of action. Here, we investigated Capsicum annuum L. seeds as a source of thermostable antifungal peptides. Thermal fractionation of a crude aqueous seed extract (RBPCE) yielded a heat-treated fraction (RBPHT) enriched in low-molecular-weight proteins. LC-MS/MS identified the type I and type II non-specific lipid-transfer proteins Ca-nsLTP1 and Ca-nsLTP2 as its predominant constituents. Compared with RBPCE, RBPHT displayed increased trypsin-inhibitory potency. RBPHT inhibited C. albicans, C. krusei, and C. auris isolates from clades I, III, and IV, including isolates showing no detectable response to fluconazole under the conditions tested. Against a representative South American clade IV isolate, the nsLTP-enriched fraction exhibited minimum inhibitory and fungicidal concentrations of 180 and 360 g/mL, respectively. RBPHT also suppressed early biofilm establishment by C. albicans and C. auris and markedly reduced viable biofilm-associated populations when applied after initial cell adhesion. These findings provide the first evidence of antifungal and antibiofilm activity by a Capsicum seed-derived nsLTP-enriched fraction against C. auris and position Ca-nsLTP1 and Ca-nsLTP2 as promising plant-derived candidates for further antifungal development.
